newsitem.title: ALBANIA: Albanians protest afresh but government unmoved.
newsitem.headline: Albanians protest afresh but government unmoved.

text.p: Albanians, angry at losing cash in a pyramid investment swindle, on Monday took to the streets in the southern town of Vlore for the 20th day while students in another town boycotted lectures in protest at the scandal.

Around 7,000 demonstrators in the Adriatic port were joined by local government staff from city hall and court offices for the daily protest march along Vlore's central palm-lined boulevard, which lasted just over an hour, witnesses said.
A young child, held aloft, carried a banner which read: "I want my daddy's money back".
The protesters gathered briefly in front of the town's university to show support for 53 students inside who have been on hunger strike since last Thursday.

The students, many with parents who lost money in collapsed pyramid schemes, have backed opposition calls for the dismissal of the right-wing Democratic Party government for failing to control the schemes or warn savers they could face losses.
In the southeastern town of Gjirokaster, near Albania's border with Greece, students boycotted lectures in solidarity with the hunger strikers and said they planned to hold a rally there on Tuesday.
"With our boycott we want to express our respect and support (the Vlore students) totally deserve," the students said in a statement.
Tirana University's faculty of electrical and mechanical engineering appealed to students nationwide to boycott classes until the government resigned.
Albania has been hit by a wave of protests and riots since five investment schemes collapsed in January leaving hundreds of thousands of ordinary people in ruin.

President Sali Berisha's government insists it is unable to reimburse savers, infuriating investors who are likely to end up with only a fraction of the cash they eagerly poured into schemes, which had offered up to 60 percent interest a month.

Berisha, who must stand for re-election by mid-March, and Prime Minister Aleksander Meksi appear prepared to ride out the storm. Protests have been disparate and sporadic and opposition parties have so far failed to turn investors' anger to their advantage.

Southern Albania, the most prosperous region in Europe's poorest state, has been worst affected by the financial scandal and has seen the most violent confrontations between protesters and riot police.
A father-of-two was killed in clashes in Vlore two weeks ago and two other men died of heart attacks. The government denies the heart attack victims were involved in the protests.

Addressing Vlore protesters on Monday, opposition Social Democrat leader Skender Gjinushi berated Berisha's record as president and said he should not stand for a second term because of the pyramid scheme scandal.
"This so-called president should not be a candidate for the second time without resolving this crisis and fulfilling your demands," he told the demonstration.

Albania's president is elected by parliament and Berisha is sure to win a second term after his Democratic Party won 122 of 140 seats in last year's general election, described by foreign observers as failing to meet international standards.
